# Section 13.1: Obtaining i.i.d. Posterior Draws

# Section 13.2: Integration Methods for Bayesian Inference

## Section 13.2.2: Laplace approximations

### Example 13.8: Road Safety data: Laplace Approximation of Marginal likelihoods
We follow up on Example 8.8 where we fitted 
two Poisson regression models to the monthly counts of children aged 6–10 that
were killed and seriously injured in Linz. In both models we included an effect
of the legal intervention. In the first model we additionally 
included a dummy variable for the holiday months July and August, whereas in the 
second model we included seasonal effects for all months.

We used the Newton-Raphson method to construct a  Normal proposal centered at 
the posterior mode for an independence Metropolis Hastings algorithm. 
We make use of this function to approximate the marginal likelihoods of the two
models using  Laplace approximation.

We first load the data and define  response, exposures and the regressor matrices of 
both models.

```{r}
data("accidents", package = "BayesianLearningCode")
y <- accidents[, "children_accidents"]
e <- accidents[, "children_exposure"]

X <- cbind(intercept = rep(1, length(y)),
           intervention = rep(c(0, 1), c(7 * 12 + 9, 8 * 12 + 3)),
           holiday = rep(rep(c(0, 1, 0), c(6, 2, 4)), 16))

seas <- rbind(diag(1, 11), rep(0, 11))
seas_dummies <- matrix(rep(t(seas), 16), ncol = 11, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(seas_dummies) <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul",
                            "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov")
X_large <- cbind(X[, -3], seas_dummies)
```

Then we implement finding of the posterior mode and computing the Laplace 
approximation.

```{r}
logmarlik_poisson <- function(y, X, e, b0 = 0, B0 = 100, t.max = 20) {
  N <- length(y)
  d <- ncol(X)

  if(length(b0==1)){
      b0<- rep(0,d)
      }
  if(length(B0==1)){
    B0 <- diag(B0, ncol=d, nrow=d)
  }
  B0.inv <- solve(B0)

  # determine the MAP
  beta_new <- matrix(c(log(mean(y/e)),rnorm(d - 1)/10), nrow = d)
  if(is.nan(beta_new[1])){
    beta.new[1]<- log(mean(y)/mean(e))
  }

  XtXi <- lapply(seq_len(N), function(i) tcrossprod(X[i,]))

  for (t in seq_len(t.max)) {
    beta_old <- beta_new

    rate <- e * exp(X %*% beta_old)
    score <- t(crossprod(y - rate, X) - t(beta_old - b0) %*% B0.inv)

    H <- -B0.inv
    for (i in seq_len(N)) {
      H <- H - rate[i] * XtXi[[i]]
    }
    beta_new <- beta_old - solve(H, score)
    if (max(abs(beta_new - beta_old)) < .Machine$double.eps) break
  }

  qmean <- beta_new

  # Determine the variance matrix
  rate <- e * exp(X %*% qmean)
  H <- -B0.inv
  for (i in seq_len(N)) {
    H <- H - rate[i] * XtXi[[i]]
  }
  qvar <- -solve(H)

  loglik<- sum(y*log(rate) - lgamma(y+1) - rate)
  lpri <-  mvtnorm::dmvnorm(t(qmean), mean = b0, sigma = B0,log = TRUE)

  lmarlik<-loglik+lpri+d/2*log(2*pi)+log(sqrt(det(qvar)))
  return(res=list(beta.post=qmean,var.beta=qvar, lmarlik=lmarlik))
}
```

We use the function to determine the approximated marginal likelihoods  for 
both models. 

```{r}
res1 <- logmarlik_poisson(y, X, e, b0 = 0, B0 = 100)
res2 <- logmarlik_poisson(y, X_large, e, b0 =0, B0 = 100)
print(c(res1$lmarlik, res2$lmarlik))
```

We clearly prefer model 1.
